champion.partB: Double-jeopardy/multiple-punishments claim preserved at Vol. 4 pp. 4–6 and re-urged at pp. 92–97; the court deferred ruling ('We can cover it later'), then denied at p. 97 on a Blockburger 'contact versus penetration' rationale. Under Patterson v. State, 152 S.W.3d 88 (Tex. Crim. App. 2004), and its progeny, indecency by contact may be subsumed as a lesser-included/incident act where the touching is part of the same continuous assaultive transaction and the State does not elect discrete acts. Here the complainant described a single uninterrupted episode in the truck cab in which the breast contact immediately preceded penetration; the State charged one date, one victim, one transaction and conceded 'we don't have multiple dates.' The error is compounded by (a) two automatic life sentences under Tex. Penal Code § 12.42(c)(2), and (b) cumulation under art. 42.08, transforming a subsumed count into a consecutive life term. Multiple-punishments double jeopardy may be raised for the first time on appeal where the violation is apparent on the face of the record (Gonzalez v. State, 8 S.W.3d 640). This is the strongest appellate issue in the record.

champion.partB: The jury assessed automatic life under Tex. Penal Code § 12.42(c)(2) on both counts and added a $10,000 fine on each. Section 12.42(c)(2) mandates 'imprisonment for life' and does not authorize a fine; a fine assessed in addition to a statutorily mandated life term is void and may be reformed or stricken on appeal or attacked as an illegal sentence at any time (Mizell v. Failure-to-investigate indicator under Strickland/Wiggins; the caller's identity and account are a concrete habeas investigation target.

challenger.quote: remote. Not an excited utterance, Judge.
challenger.partA: The judge let the mother repeat what her daughter told her about being raped, even though it happened 15–20 minutes or more after the events, under a rule for statements made in the heat of the moment. The defense objected that too much time had passed. This was saved for appeal.
challenger.partB: Hearsay objections to Jennifer Stutts relaying the complainant's rape allegation were overruled under the excited-utterance exception despite a documented 15–20+ minute interval and intervening events; similar excited-utterance rulings admitted Evan Perry's account. Preserved Rule 803(2) issue; likely reviewed for abuse of discretion and harm, but relevant to the cumulative prior-consistent-statement strategy the State employed throughout.

challenger.quote: A. I can't compare it.
challenger.partA: The automatic life sentence depended on proving Mr. Ellis is the same man convicted in a 1986 case. The State's own fingerprint expert admitted he could not compare the old fingerprints to Mr. Ellis's because of scarring and bad print quality. The State relied instead on matching ID numbers on paperwork. Whether that was enough proof is worth a close look.
challenger.partB: The mandatory-life enhancement under Tex. Penal Code 12.42(c)(2) rested on the 1986 burglary-with-intent-to-commit-sexual-assault pen packet, yet Investigator Goodwin admitted he could not make any fingerprint comparison to State's 39 or 40 due to scarring/microfilm distortion; linkage was established solely through FBI/SID/SSN identifiers across a sex-offender packet and jail cards. While Texas permits identity proof by totality (Flowers v. State), the sufficiency of the linkage evidence for the true finding — and counsel's handling of it (no directed-verdict motion at punishment) — warrants appellate/habeas evaluation given the defendant pleaded 'not true.'

challenger.quote: her. It's about the people that live in this county.
challenger.partA: At sentencing, the prosecutor asked jurors to think about their own kids and grandkids and the people of the county when deciding punishment, and reminded them how fast they had found him guilty. Arguments like that appeal to fear and community pressure rather than the evidence. The defense did not object.
challenger.partB: Punishment summation included community-expectation and fear-based appeals ('It's about us. It's about her. It's about the people that live in this county,' driving past the scene with 'your kid or grandkid'), plus commentary praising the speed of the guilt deliberations. No objections were made, forfeiting review; contributes to a cumulative unobjected-argument IAC claim at the punishment phase where consecutive life sentences were assessed.

challenger.quote: directed verdict is denied.
challenger.partA: After the State finished its case, the defense asked the judge to end the case because the accuser never said exactly where the assault happened, and the crime must be proven to have happened in San Jacinto County. The judge refused. This request was made on the record and saved.
challenger.partB: Counsel moved for directed verdict on venue/county-of-offense grounds, arguing the complainant described only 'a sandy area' and never placed the assault in San Jacinto County except via the defendant's alleged statement and the State's cell-site/photo reconstruction; denied. Preserved sufficiency-of-venue issue (venue requires only preponderance under Art. 13.17, so likely weak standing alone, but properly part of the appellate matrix).

challenger.quote: That phone number was (903) 452-4609, correct?
challenger.partA: During the investigation, someone called the detective and suggested the girl might be lying about what happened. The detective talked to that caller briefly, but never found out who she was and never followed up on it. The jury heard almost nothing about this.
challenger.partB: On cross, Sgt. Sheikh conceded that on or about July 15, 2022 he received a call from an unidentified female at (903) 452-4609 constituting 'an allegation... that Daisy could be lying about this,' that the caller 'did not identify herself,' and that he conducted no further investigation (Excerpts 275-277). Counsel should confirm whether any report, recording, CAD entry, or notes memorializing this exculpatory lead were disclosed under Brady/art. 39.14, and whether the tipster was ever identified.

challenger.quote: A. I don't know what this is. I'm sorry.
challenger.partA: When the lawyers were looking at the phone records at trial, the prosecutor handed over two extra stacks of papers. The lead detective said he had never seen them and didn't know what they were. That raises a question about whether all the phone records were shared before trial.
challenger.partB: During voir dire on State's 18-19, defense counsel was handed 'two other packets' apparently from the AT&T production; the case agent testified he had never seen them and could not identify them. This raises a question whether the complete CDR return (call detail, per-call tower data, carrier disclaimers) was timely produced and authenticated, and whether the admitted exhibits were a curated subset.

challenger.quote: I have a stack of about 20 pages that
challenger.partA: The prosecutor admitted he had about 20 more pages of phone-record data in his file that were never shown to the jury. He described them as hard to read and said they were not as neat as the summary that was used in court.
challenger.partB: The prosecutor stated on the record that his file contained approximately 20 additional pages of raw AT&T data ('some kind of gibberish') that were 'part of the file' but 'not as concise a summary as what's marked as State's 19.' Counsel should obtain and compare the full raw production against the admitted summary map (State's 18) for material discrepancies, including the acknowledged conflict with video timestamps.

challenger.quote: A. I know it was collected from the underwear.
challenger.partA: The lab collected small pieces of material (like hairs or fibers) from the girl's underwear, but nobody ever tested them. So no one knows what that evidence would have shown.
challenger.partB: DPS analyst Solis confirmed trace evidence was collected from the complainant's underwear but never analyzed because the agency never requested trace examination. This is untested physical evidence in State custody with potential exculpatory or corroborative value; counsel should confirm its preservation, chain of custody, and whether testing (or Chapter 64-type analysis) remains available.

challenger.quote: no swabs were present inside the swab box
challenger.partA: One of the swabs from the hospital exam kit — the one from the outside genital area — was missing when the lab opened the box. The box was labeled for that swab, but nothing was inside, so it was never tested.
challenger.partB: Per the biology analyst's notes read into the record, the vulvar swab envelope in the SANE kit was empty ('no swabs were present inside the swab box') despite the check-box and SANE labeling, so no analysis was performed on item 01-03. This documents a chain-of-custody/evidence-integrity gap in the kit that was not otherwise explained; counsel should reconcile the SANE collection log (State's 20) against the DPS intake itemization.

challenger.quote: photos that may or may not get sent over with
challenger.partA: The nurse took detailed medical photographs during the exam with a special high-resolution camera, but those photos were not shown at trial and may not have been given out with the medical chart. The nurse said she keeps such photos guarded.
challenger.partB: SANE Schofield testified she used an SDFI camera setup and took photographs (including of the genital exam and the petechiae) that 'may or may not get sent over with the medical chart,' and the prosecutor's phrasing ('even if they were here') indicates the colposcope/SDFI photographs were not present at trial. Counsel should confirm whether the photographic documentation referenced in the 'Forensic exam. Photo documentation' summary was disclosed, and whether it corroborates or contradicts the no-acute-trauma findings.

challenger.quote: and he's staying there until 9:35. That's not accurate,
challenger.partA: The State's own map of the phone signals said the truck arrived in Livingston minutes after the McDonald's camera showed it was already there. The detective admitted on the stand that the phone-location data was not accurate.
challenger.partB: Sgt. Sheikh conceded the cell-site plotting (State's 18/19) was inaccurate: the McDonald's video shows the truck at 9:15 p.m., while the mapped pings place the phone arriving at 9:21 and remaining until 9:35 — 'That's not accurate, is it? A. No.' This admission undercuts the State's '29-minute gap' venue/opportunity theory, which was derived by a non-expert using a free coordinate-plotting website, over a preserved reliability objection.

challenger.quote: I do not have her name
challenger.partA: The DNA witness admitted she did not personally do the lab steps that pulled the DNA out of the samples. A different lab worker did that, and the witness could not even say that worker's name in court.
challenger.partB: Analyst Solis testified the extraction (and other bench work) was performed by a third, unnamed qualified analyst — not Solis and not Patnaik — whose identity was not in her materials ('I do not have her name with me'). Combined with the preserved Confrontation Clause objection to Solis testifying to Patnaik's screening (overruled), counsel should confirm whether the identities, bench notes, and proficiency/CV materials of all analysts in the testing chain were disclosed.

challenger.quote: stuff in here that's not very complimentary of my
challenger.partA: The prosecutor told the judge that the girl's counseling records contained a lot of negative information about her, and that she 'has lots of problems.' Those records were never put in front of the jury.
challenger.partB: The State acknowledged on the record that the Burke Center counseling records in its possession contained material 'not very complimentary of my victim' and that the complainant 'obviously has lots of problems'; the records were never admitted. This is a prosecutorial admission that credibility-impeaching material exists in the State's file; counsel should verify complete production of the Burke/therapy records (including the September 2022 social-worker entries cross-examined from) under Brady/Giglio and art. 39.14.

challenger.quote: sometimes Daisy is lying to you and you don't find
challenger.partA: The girl's own mother agreed that, according to therapy records, she had told a worker that her daughter sometimes lies to her and she doesn't find out until later. The mother also said at the McDonald's, 'if this is for real,' meaning she did not believe her daughter at first.
challenger.partB: Jennifer Stutts admitted the substance of therapy-record entries: that Daisy 'is lying to you and you don't find out about it until later on' (answered 'Yes'), plus her contemporaneous conditional statement ('if this is for real, I'm taking you straight to the hospital'). These record-based admissions are specific impeachment of the complainant's credibility sourced to documents not in evidence; confirm full disclosure of the underlying therapy/social-worker records.

challenger.quote: A. They did not. They did not follow the
challenger.partA: When the defendant was arrested, the detective had asked the arresting police department to grab the truck and his phone, because both could hold important evidence. That department did not follow those instructions, so the truck was never searched and the phone was never taken.
challenger.partB: Sgt. Sheikh testified he placed TCIC instructions for Spring Valley PD to tow the vehicle and seize the defendant's phone upon arrest; the agency 'did not follow the instructions.' The alleged crime-scene vehicle interior and the device itself were thus never collected or examined — potentially exculpatory physical evidence (e.g., transfer-DNA and interior corroboration issues) lost through State-side failure; assess under Brady/Youngblood and as an ineffective-investigation avenue.

challenger.quote: A. Back seat.
challenger.partA: The girl's friend at McDonald's said she told him the assault happened in the back seat of the truck, and that she went to the restroom when she arrived. At trial, the girl said it happened in the front passenger seat and that she never went to the restroom. Those stories don't match.
challenger.partB: Evan Perry testified the complainant reported the assault occurred in the 'back seat' of the truck and that she went to the restroom at McDonald's; the complainant testified it occurred in 'the passenger's side front seat' and denied using the restroom ('No, sir, I did not,' Excerpt 415), a denial also contradicted by Sheikh. These are concrete prior-inconsistent-statement impeachment points on core details of the account.

challenger.quote: Never heard that before.
challenger.partA: In closing, the defense lawyer said the girl's trial claim — that she left because of suicidal thoughts and cyberbullying that day — was brand new. He said he had reviewed all the evidence and had never heard that explanation before trial.
challenger.partB: Defense counsel represented in summation that the complainant's trial explanation for walking away (same-day suicidal ideation and cyberbullying) appeared for the first time at trial and was absent from all prior statements he had reviewed ('Never heard that before... And I've seen all the evidence'). This flags either a material inconsistency across the CAC interview, SANE history, and police statements, or a disclosure gap; the underlying statements should be compared.

challenger.quote: A. I didn't make a comparison due to the
challenger.partA: The automatic life sentence depended on proving an old 1986 conviction belonged to the same man. The State's fingerprint expert admitted he could not compare the fingerprints on those old records because of scarring and poor print quality, so identity rested only on matching ID numbers and photos.
challenger.partB: Investigator Goodwin conceded he made no fingerprint comparison linking the defendant to the 1986 Burglary of a Habitation w/ Intent to Commit Sexual Assault pen packet (State's 39) or the enhancement judgments, due to thumb scarring and microfilm-degraded prints; the automatic-life enhancement therefore rested on FBI/SID/DL identifiers and photographs, with preserved objections to the pen-packet declarations' completeness. This is a sufficiency/identity-of-priors issue central to the mandatory life sentences imposed on both counts.

challenger.quote: It's a free website. It offers a free service
challenger.partA: The detective made the map that supposedly showed where the phone went by typing numbers into a free website he found online. He is not a phone-tracking expert, and the phone company itself says its location data is only approximate. A map built this way can look scientific to a jury even though no trained expert ever checked it.
challenger.partB: Sgt. Sheikh, a non-expert, generated State's Exhibit 18 by plotting AT&T CDR coordinates on 'Batchego.com,' a free consumer website, with no validation, error-rate testing, or peer-reviewed methodology (RR3 at 169-174). Historical cell-site analysis presented through a lay officer implicates Tex. R. Evid. 702/Kelly reliability requirements and Art. 11.073's contemplation of methods whose reliability has been materially undermined; the granularity claims (a 29-minute 'gap' proving a stop at FM 945/SH 156) exceed what single-tower CDR data can scientifically support.

challenger.quote: You've never testified as a cell phone expert?
challenger.partA: The defense lawyer objected that the detective was not qualified to explain cell phone tower records or the map he made from them, but the judge let the evidence in anyway. That objection was made on the record, which matters because it keeps the issue alive for appeal.
challenger.partB: Defense voir dire established Sheikh had never testified as a cell-site expert and could not testify to the mapping or the AT&T records as an expert; counsel objected to relevance, incompleteness, and the witness's qualifications as to State's 18 and 19, and the objection was overruled (RR3 at 172-173). This preserves a Rule 702/Kelly gatekeeping challenge to the admission of lay-generated cell-site location evidence used to establish venue and the timeline.

challenger.quote: and he's staying there until 9:35. That's not accurate,
challenger.partA: On cross-examination, the detective admitted his phone-location timeline was wrong: his cell data said the truck arrived at the McDonald's six minutes after the security video actually showed it arriving. Even so, the State used the same phone data to argue there was a 29-minute 'missing' period proving a stop where the crime supposedly happened.
challenger.partB: Sheikh conceded on cross that the CDR-derived location times conflicted with the McDonald's surveillance video (9:21-9:35 pings vs. 9:15 video arrival) and were 'not accurate' (RR3 at 207), and that AT&T explicitly disclaims precise use of its coordinates (RR3 at 206). Yet the State relied on the same data for the 29-minute-gap inference and venue in San Jacinto County. The internal inconsistency undermines the reliability of the cell-site evidence under Kelly/Rule 702 and supports an 11.073 development theory regarding overstated CSLI precision.

challenger.quote: the improper witness to talk about the DNA testing in
challenger.partA: The DNA witness who testified did not do the actual lab work. Another analyst did the first screening and a third, unnamed analyst did the extraction, but neither came to court. The defense objected that Mr. Ellis never got to question the people who actually handled and tested the evidence, and the judge overruled that objection.
challenger.partB: Counsel objected under the Confrontation Clause that Solis was 'the improper witness' because Patnaik performed the biological screening (State's 33, 35) and an unidentified analyst performed extraction/amplification; the objections were overruled and the surrogate testified to the absent analysts' work (RR3 at 33-35, 38-39, 57). Under Smith v. Arizona, 602 U.S. 779 (2024), a surrogate analyst's conveyance of an absent analyst's testimonial statements for their truth violates the Sixth Amendment; this issue is preserved and directly cognizable on appeal or in post-conviction review.

challenger.quote: odds of it belonging, saliva, to this defendant 1 in
challenger.partA: In his opening, the prosecutor told the jury the DNA numbers meant 'it's him' — the defendant — period. But the lab's own numbers are 'likelihood ratios,' which compare two scenarios; they are not a statement that the DNA definitely came from one person. Saying the number proves identity overstates what the science actually says.
challenger.partB: The prosecutor converted the lab's likelihood ratios into categorical source attribution ('1 in 16.8 septillion... it's him. I mean that's the guy'), whereas the analyst's reports used LR verbal-scale language ('support for the proposition that Gary Ellis is a possible contributor'). No contemporaneous objection was lodged, so the claim is unpreserved as trial error, but the transposition of an LR into an identity statement is a recognized form of overstated forensic-identification argument (prosecutor's fallacy) relevant to cumulative-prejudice and IAC analyses.

challenger.quote: Most of the time they lie to get out of
challenger.partA: The forensic interviewer told the jury that in her experience, when kids lie, they usually lie to get out of trouble — not to get into it. Because the accuser here would be 'getting into' something by reporting, this kind of statement quietly tells the jury the accuser is probably truthful. Courts have said experts are not allowed to vouch for whether a witness is telling the truth.
challenger.partB: Forensic interviewer Carmona, drawing on '3,427' interviews, testified that children usually lie to get out of trouble rather than into it (RR3 at 218-219) — class-based truthfulness testimony that functions as indirect bolstering of the complainant, prohibited under Yount v. State, 872 S.W.2d 706 (Tex. Crim. App. 1993) and Schutz v. State, 957 S.W.2d 52 (Tex. Crim. App. 1997). The specific question drew no truthfulness-based objection, so review would proceed via IAC or in combination with other bolstering (Sheikh's expert-framed testimony on child consistency).

challenger.quote: This is, and I'm probably not qualified to
challenger.partA: The detective started to explain how children's memories work, then admitted mid-answer he was 'probably not qualified' to say. The prosecutor then re-framed him as an 'expert' on child demeanor and got him to tell the jury it is normal for a child's story to change. That let a police officer bolster the accuser's shifting accounts without real expert qualifications.
challenger.partB: Sheikh conceded 'I'm probably not qualified' to opine on children's memory, after which the State elicited that he had previously testified 'as an expert on the demeanor and existence or lack of existence of physical [evidence] in other sex abuse cases' and had him normalize inconsistencies in child accounts (RR3 at 119-120). Admission of law-enforcement opinion normalizing complainant inconsistency without Rule 702 qualification is bolstering; the defense objection to the memory answer was lodged but the reframed line proceeded, warranting evaluation for preservation and IAC.

challenger.quote: I can't compare it.
challenger.partA: At punishment, the State's fingerprint examiner admitted he could not match Mr. Ellis's fingerprints to the paperwork from the 1986 conviction — the very conviction that triggered an automatic life sentence. The jury found it was the same person anyway, based on things like an FBI number and old photos rather than a fingerprint match.
challenger.partB: Investigator Goodwin testified he could not compare the prints on the 1986 burglary-with-intent-to-commit-sexual-assault pen packet (State's 39) or on other Harris County records to the defendant's known 10-print card due to scarring and microfilm degradation (RR5 at 20, 34-36), yet the enhancement finding produced mandatory life under Penal Code § 12.42(c)(2). While Flowers v. State, 220 S.W.3d 919 (Tex. Crim. App. 2007) permits linkage by non-fingerprint identifiers (FBI/SID numbers, photographs), the absence of any print match, coupled with the defendant's 'not true' plea and preserved objections to the pen packets' completeness, makes sufficiency of the enhancement linkage a viable appellate issue to evaluate.

challenger.quote: And then through facial recognition with
challenger.partA: The police identified Mr. Ellis as the suspect by running gas-station video stills through facial recognition software at another county's office. Facial recognition has known error problems, and here the same identification was then reinforced by a photo lineup shown to the accuser. If the software picked the wrong man, everything after it would be built on that mistake.
challenger.partB: Suspect development rested on facial-recognition analysis of Valero surveillance stills performed by Montgomery County analyst Katricia Hortman (RR3 at 130-132, 191-192), which then seeded the photospread from which the complainant identified Ellis. Facial-recognition-generated leads are an emerging reliability concern (no validated error rates disclosed, no Daubert/Kelly hearing conducted, algorithm and candidate list undisclosed), relevant to an Art. 11.073/Brady-adjacent investigation into the software used, its outputs, and any non-disclosed alternative candidates, though the strong corroborating DNA evidence limits materiality.

challenger.quote: sentence you to life in prison with a $10,000 fine
challenger.partA: The judge gave a life sentence on each count and also added a $10,000 fine on each count. But under the Texas law that required the automatic life sentence, a money fine is likely not allowed at all. If that is right, the fines are illegal and a court could strike them from the judgment.
challenger.partB: The trial court imposed a $10,000 fine on each count in addition to mandatory life sentences assessed under Tex. Penal Code § 12.42(c)(2) (prior conviction for Burglary of a Habitation with Intent to Commit Sexual Assault, Cause No. 431106, 184th Dist. Ct., Harris County, 2/11/1986). Section 12.42(c)(2) prescribes only imprisonment for life and, unlike § 12.42(c)(1), contains no fine provision. Under the line of authority holding that mandatory-life enhancement statutes silent as to fines do not authorize a fine (cf. cases deleting fines under § 12.42(d) and § 12.42(c)(2)), both $10,000 fines are unauthorized punishment—an illegal-sentence defect cognizable at any time and remediable by judgment reformation deleting the fines on Counts I and II.

challenger.quote: fine not to exceed $10,000.00 may be imposed.
challenger.partA: The written instructions given to the jury told them they could add a fine of up to $10,000 even when the law required an automatic life sentence. That instruction likely invited the jury to assess a fine the law does not permit, which is how the possibly illegal fines ended up in the verdict.
challenger.partB: The punishment charge instructed the jury that, upon finding the § 12.42(c)(2) enhancement true, it must assess life confinement 'and a fine not to exceed $10,000.00 may be imposed.' If § 12.42(c)(2) authorizes only life imprisonment, this instruction authorized punishment outside the statutory range, constituting charge error that produced the unauthorized $10,000 fines assessed on both counts; supports the illegal-sentence/judgment-reformation claim and, alternatively, an Almanza egregious-harm analysis as to the fines.

challenger.quote: I can't compare it.
challenger.partA: The automatic life sentence depended on proving a 1986 conviction belonged to Mr. Ellis. The State's own fingerprint expert admitted he could not match the fingerprints on that old prison packet to Mr. Ellis because of scarring and poor print quality. The State instead relied on things like an FBI number and photos. Whether that other proof was legally enough to trigger the automatic life sentence is a question a lawyer should examine.
challenger.partB: The § 12.42(c)(2) enhancement (Cause No. 431106, 1986 burglary with intent to commit sexual assault) was the sole predicate for the mandatory life sentences, and the defendant pleaded 'not true.' The State's fingerprint examiner, Investigator Goodwin, conceded on voir dire/cross that he could not compare the prints in the 1986 pen packet (State's 39) to the known 10-print card (38A), and likewise could not match the right thumbprint on the prohibited-weapon judgment due to scarring/distortion. Identity was proven only circumstantially through FBI/SID numbers, SSN, and photographs. Counsel should evaluate a legal-sufficiency challenge to the enhancement finding under Flowers v. State, 220 S.W.3d 919 (Tex. Crim. App. 2007) (totality-of-the-evidence linkage), recognizing Flowers permits non-fingerprint linkage but the record here rests heavily on documentary identifiers the sponsoring witness did not independently verify.

challenger.quote: indecency with a child by contact is a lesser included
challenger.partA: The defense argued that the second charge (touching the breast) was really part of the same act as the first charge (the sexual assault), so punishing him twice for one event might be unfair double punishment. The judge disagreed, and the jury gave two life sentences that run one after the other. This objection was made on the record, so an appeals lawyer can raise it.
challenger.partB: Defense counsel preserved a multiple-punishments double-jeopardy/lesser-included objection to submission of Count II (indecency by contact—breast touching) alongside Count I (sexual assault by penetration) arising from a single episode; the court overruled it applying Blockburger. Counsel should analyze whether the breast contact was 'incident to and subsumed by' the penetration under Patterson v. State, 152 S.W.3d 88 (Tex. Crim. App. 2004) and progeny; the complainant's testimony describes breast touching as a discrete preparatory act, which likely defeats subsumption, but the issue is preserved and directly affects the second life sentence and the cumulation order.

challenger.quote: sentences run consecutively
challenger.partA: The judge ordered the two life sentences to run back-to-back instead of at the same time. For these particular crimes against a child, Texas law does allow stacking, so this is probably legal—but the paperwork should be checked to make sure the written judgment matches exactly what the judge said in court.
challenger.partB: The trial court granted the State's motion to cumulate and orally ordered the Count II sentence to run consecutively to Count I. Stacking appears authorized by Tex. Penal Code § 3.03(b)(2)(A) for §§ 22.011 and 21.11 offenses against a victim younger than 17 tried in a single criminal action, so the cumulation is likely lawful; however, counsel should verify (1) that the written judgments contain a sufficiently specific cumulation order consistent with the oral pronouncement (Ex parte Madding), and (2) that stacking of two mandatory life terms plus the unauthorized fines is accurately reflected, since any variance between oral pronouncement and written judgment controls in favor of the oral pronouncement.
